outcomes.text: Understand base units, the nature of measurement errors and their numerical treatment, and estimation.
Use base SI units (mass, length, time, amount of substance, temperature, current) and derived units.
Use SI prefixes T to f and standard form, and convert between units such as J and eV, J and kWh.
Identify random and systematic errors and ways to reduce them; distinguish precision, repeatability, reproducibility, resolution and accuracy.
Combine absolute, fractional and percentage uncertainties.
Show uncertainty with error bars and find uncertainties in gradient and intercept.
Estimate physical quantities to the nearest order of magnitude and derive further estimates.
Understand fundamental properties of matter, electromagnetic radiation and quantum phenomena.
Describe the particles that make up atoms and how they interact.
Describe the proton, neutron and electron model with charge and mass in SI and relative units.
Calculate specific charge of protons, electrons, nuclei and ions.
Use proton number, nucleon number, nuclide notation and isotope data.
Explain the strong nuclear force: attraction to about 3 fm, repulsion below 0.5 fm.
Write equations for alpha and beta-minus decay, including the neutrino.
Compare particles with antiparticles in mass, charge and rest energy; know the antiparticle pairs.
Use the photon model E = hf = hc/wavelength.
Describe annihilation and pair production and their energies.
Name the four fundamental interactions and explain exchange particles.
Describe the electromagnetic force (virtual photons) and the weak interaction (W bosons) in beta decay, electron capture and electron-proton collisions.
Draw simple Feynman-style diagrams of these interactions.
Classify hadrons as baryons and mesons; apply baryon number conservation.
Describe leptons (electron, muon, neutrino) and lepton number conservation.
Explain strange particles and strangeness conservation in strong and weak interactions.
State charge, baryon number and strangeness of up, down and strange quarks and antiquarks.
Build baryons, antibaryons and mesons from quarks and describe neutron decay.
Describe quark character change in beta decay.
Apply conservation of charge, baryon number, lepton number, strangeness, energy and momentum to interactions.
Describe evidence for quantum behaviour of light and matter.
Explain threshold frequency, work function and stopping potential with the photon model.
Use the photoelectric equation hf = work function + maximum kinetic energy.
Explain ionisation and excitation, including in a fluorescent tube.
Use the electron volt and convert between eV and J.
Explain line spectra as evidence of discrete energy levels.
Use hf = E1 - E2 with energies in J or eV.
Explain how electron diffraction and the photoelectric effect show wave and particle behaviour.
Use the de Broglie wavelength h/mv and explain how diffraction depends on momentum.
Extend GCSE wave ideas to travelling and stationary waves, refraction, diffraction, superposition and interference.
Describe progressive and stationary waves.
Describe amplitude, frequency, wavelength, speed and phase difference (in radians, degrees or cycles); use c = f lambda and f = 1/T.
Distinguish longitudinal and transverse waves, with sound, electromagnetic and string examples, and the speed of EM waves in a vacuum.
Explain polarisation as evidence for transverse waves and its applications (Polaroid, aerial alignment).
Explain stationary waves from two waves of equal frequency in opposite directions, with nodes and antinodes, graphically.
Use f = (1/2l) sqrt(T/mu) for the first harmonic and describe harmonics on strings, microwaves and sound.
Required practical 1: investigate stationary wave frequency against length, tension and mass per unit length.
Describe interference, diffraction and refraction of waves.
Explain path difference and coherence, and Young's double-slit interference with a laser or white light; use fringe spacing w = lambda D / s.
Describe interference with sound and electromagnetic waves and lasers safely.
Required practical 2: investigate interference with Young's slits and a diffraction grating.
Describe single-slit diffraction patterns and how central maximum width varies with wavelength and slit width.
Use a diffraction grating at normal incidence: d sin(theta) = n lambda, and its applications.
Use refractive index n = c/cs and Snell's law n1 sin(theta1) = n2 sin(theta2).
Explain total internal reflection (sin thetac = n2/n1) and step-index optical fibres including cladding.
Explain material and modal dispersion, pulse broadening and absorption.
Study vectors, forces, energy, momentum and bulk properties of materials.
Apply forces, energy and momentum to motion.
Distinguish scalars and vectors and add vectors by calculation or scale drawing.
Resolve vectors into perpendicular components, including on an inclined plane.
Apply conditions for equilibrium of two or three coplanar forces.
Define moment and couple; apply the principle of moments.
Use centre of mass, which for a uniform regular solid is at its centre.
Use displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration, and their graphs and areas and gradients.
Use v = u + at, s = (u+v)t/2, s = ut + at^2/2 and v^2 = u^2 + 2as.
Required practical 3: determine g by a free-fall method.
Treat horizontal and vertical motion independently in a uniform gravitational field.
Describe friction, lift, drag, terminal speed and effects of air resistance qualitatively.
Apply Newton's three laws, including F = ma for constant mass.
Use momentum, conservation of linear momentum in one dimension and F = change in mv / change in t.
Use impulse, force-time graphs and impact forces; distinguish elastic and inelastic collisions and explosions.
Calculate work W = Fs cos(theta), power P = W/t = Fv, and area under force-displacement graphs.
Calculate efficiency as useful output over input.
Apply energy conservation using change in Ep = mg change in h and Ek = mv^2/2, including resistive work.
Describe bulk properties of materials.
Use density rho = m/V.
Use Hooke's law, elastic limit, stiffness, F = k change in L, tensile stress and strain, breaking stress.
Calculate elastic strain energy (1/2 F change in L) and interpret force-extension and stress-strain graphs, plastic and brittle behaviour.
Use Young modulus = stress/strain and stress-strain graphs.
Required practical 4: determine the Young modulus by a simple method.
Build on GCSE electricity to study circuits.
Study current electricity.
Define current as rate of flow of charge, I = dQ/dt, potential difference as W/Q, and resistance R = V/I.
Describe I-V characteristics of an ohmic conductor, semiconductor diode and filament lamp, and Ohm's law as a special case.
Use resistivity rho = RA/L.
Describe temperature effects on metals and ntc thermistors and thermistor applications.
Describe superconductivity, critical temperature and applications.
Required practical 5: determine resistivity of a wire.
Combine resistors in series and parallel.
Use E = IVt and P = IV = I^2R = V^2/R.
Apply conservation of charge and energy in dc circuits, including cells in series and parallel.
Use a potential divider with variable resistors, thermistors and LDRs to supply constant or variable pd.
Use emf, terminal pd and epsilon = E/Q = I(R + r) with non-negligible internal resistance.
Required practical 6: investigate emf and internal resistance of cells.
Extend mechanics to circular motion and SHM, and study thermal properties, ideal gases and kinetic theory.
Describe circular motion and simple harmonic motion.
Explain that circular motion needs a centripetal force; use angular speed omega = v/r = 2 pi f and radians.
Use a = v^2/r = omega^2 r and F = mv^2/r = m omega^2 r.
State the SHM condition a is proportional to -x with a = -omega^2 x.
Use x = A cos(omega t), v = +/- omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2), max speed omega A and max acceleration omega^2 A.
Sketch and relate x, v and a graphs against time.
Use T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k) for a mass-spring and T = 2 pi sqrt(l/g) for a simple pendulum (small-angle approximation).
Describe variation of Ek, Ep and total energy, and effects of damping.
Required practical 7: investigate SHM with a mass-spring system and a pendulum.
Describe free and forced vibrations, resonance and how damping affects sharpness of resonance.
Describe thermal energy, ideal gases and kinetic theory.
Define internal energy and explain how heating and work change it (qualitative first law).
Use Q = mc change in theta and Q = ml, including continuous flow, and explain energy changes in a change of state.
Describe gas laws, absolute zero and use pV = nRT and pV = NkT.
Calculate work done p change in V; use Avogadro constant, molar gas constant, Boltzmann constant, molar and molecular mass.
Required practical 8: investigate Boyle's and Charles's laws.
Explain Brownian motion as evidence for atoms and gas laws via a molecular model.
Derive and use pV = (1/3) N m c_rms^2 and average molecular kinetic energy = (3/2)kT.
Unify gravitational, electric and magnetic fields and study orbits, capacitors and induction.
Describe a force field as a region of non-contact force, represented as a vector.
Compare gravitational and electrostatic forces: inverse-square laws and field lines, but charges can repel.
Describe gravitational fields.
Use F = Gm1m2/r^2 for point masses.
Represent fields with field lines; use g = F/m and g = GM/r^2 in a radial field.
Define gravitational potential and potential difference, work change in W = m change in V, and equipotentials.
Use V = -GM/r and g = -change in V / change in r; interpret graphs of g and V against r.
Relate orbital period and speed to radius, including T^2 proportional to r^3.
Describe energy of satellites, escape velocity, synchronous and geostationary orbits.
Describe electric fields.
Use F = Q1Q2/(4 pi epsilon0 r^2) and compare gravitational and electrostatic forces between subatomic particles.
Represent fields with lines; use E = F/Q, E = V/d in uniform fields and E = Q/(4 pi epsilon0 r^2) in radial fields.
Describe the path of a charge entering a uniform field at right angles.
Define electric potential and difference; use change in W = Q change in V, equipotentials, V = Q/(4 pi epsilon0 r) and E = -change in V / change in r; interpret graphs.
Study capacitors.
Define capacitance C = Q/V.
Use C = A epsilon0 epsilon_r / d, relative permittivity and dielectric action of polar molecules.
Interpret area under a Q-V graph and use E = QV/2 = CV^2/2 = Q^2/2C.
Interpret Q, V and I graphs for charging and discharging; use the time constant RC and T1/2 = 0.69RC.
Use Q = Q0 e^(-t/RC) and charging equation with V and I forms.
Required practical 9: investigate capacitor charge and discharge using log-linear plots.
Study magnetic fields, induction and alternating current.
Use F = BIl, Fleming's left-hand rule and the tesla.
Required practical 10: investigate force on a wire with a top-pan balance.

subtopics.title: Moving charges in a magnetic field

outcomes.text: Use F = BQv, force direction on positive and negative charges, circular paths and the cyclotron.
Define flux = BA and flux linkage N flux; use flux linkage = BAN cos(theta) for a rotating coil.
Required practical 11: investigate flux linkage and coil angle with a search coil.
Apply Faraday's and Lenz's laws and emf = N change in flux / change in t.
Calculate emf in a moving conductor and a rotating coil: emf = BANomega sin(omega t).
Use rms, peak and peak-to-peak values for sinusoidal ac: Irms = I0/sqrt2, Vrms = V0/sqrt2; mains values.
Use an oscilloscope as ac/dc voltmeter and to measure time and frequency.
Use Ns/Np = Vs/Vp and efficiency IsVs/IpVp; explain eddy currents and inefficiencies.
Calculate power loss in high-voltage transmission.
Link the nucleus to nuclear power through radioactivity, nuclear energy and mass.
Describe radioactivity.
Describe Rutherford scattering and how understanding of the nucleus changed over time.
Describe properties and experimental identification of alpha, beta and gamma radiation, their hazards and uses such as thickness gauging.
Use the inverse-square law for gamma radiation I = k/x^2 and apply it to safe handling; allow for background radiation.
Weigh risks and benefits of radiation in medicine.
Required practical 12: investigate the inverse-square law for gamma radiation.
Explain random decay with constant decay probability; use dN/dt = -lambda N and N = N0 e^(-lambda t).
Use activity A = lambda N and A = A0 e^(-lambda t), with molar mass or Avogadro constant.
Use half-life T1/2 = ln2/lambda and find it from decay and log graphs; apply to waste storage and dating.
Interpret the N-Z graph of stable nuclei and decay modes (alpha, beta+, beta-, electron capture).
Write decay equations and use nuclear energy level diagrams; describe gamma emission and technetium-99m.
Estimate radius from closest approach of alpha particles and from electron diffraction.
Use R = R0 A^(1/3) as evidence for constant nuclear density and calculate nuclear density.
Use E = mc^2, mass difference, binding energy, the atomic mass unit (1 u = 931.5 MeV).
Describe fission and fusion, calculate energy released, and read the binding energy per nucleon graph.
Explain thermal-neutron fission, chain reactions and critical mass.
Explain the roles and materials of moderator, control rods and coolant in a thermal reactor.
Describe fuel handling, shielding, emergency shut-down and radioactive waste production, handling and storage.
Weigh risks and benefits of nuclear power.
Apply physics to the Universe and the devices used to observe it.
Describe telescopes.
Draw ray diagrams in normal adjustment and use angular magnification M = fo/fe.
Describe the Cassegrain arrangement and compare reflectors with refractors, including spherical and chromatic aberration.

subtopics.title: Radio, infrared, ultraviolet and X-ray telescopes

outcomes.text: Compare radio telescopes with optical telescopes in structure, positioning, use, resolving and collecting power.
Use the Rayleigh criterion theta = lambda/D; collecting power is proportional to diameter squared.
Compare the eye and CCD as detectors in quantum efficiency, resolution and convenience.
Classify stars.
Use apparent magnitude and the Hipparcos scale: a difference of 1 is an intensity ratio of 2.51.
Use parsec, light year and absolute magnitude with m - M = 5 log(d/10).
Use Wien's law (lambda_max T = 2.9e-3 m K) and Stefan's law P = sigma A T^4 treating stars as black bodies; apply the inverse-square law.
Describe spectral classes O, B, A, F, G, K, M by colour, temperature and absorption lines, and Balmer lines (n = 2).
Describe the HR diagram: main sequence, dwarfs, giants, the Sun's position, and the evolution of a Sun-like star to a white dwarf.

subtopics.title: Supernovae, neutron stars and black holes

outcomes.text: Describe supernovae, neutron stars, black holes, gamma-ray bursts and supermassive black holes.
Use type 1a supernovae as standard candles, with dark energy and acceleration.
Calculate the Schwarzschild radius Rs = 2GM/c^2.
Describe the origin and structure of the Universe.
Use delta f / f = v/c and z = delta lambda / lambda = -v/c for v much less than c; analyse binary stars, galaxies and quasars.
Use v = Hd and estimate the age of the universe; describe the Big Bang evidence: microwave background and hydrogen/helium abundance.
Describe quasars as distant, bright, red-shifted radio sources powered by active supermassive black holes.
Describe why direct detection is hard and the radial velocity (Doppler) and transit methods with a typical light curve.
Apply physics to the eye, ear, imaging and therapy.
Describe the physics of the eye.
Describe the eye as a refracting system with ray diagrams, its sensitivity and spatial resolution (rods and cones).
Use lens power P = 1/f, 1/u + 1/v = 1/f and m = v/u.
Describe myopia, hypermetropia and astigmatism and calculate corrective lens powers.
Describe the physics of the ear.
Describe the structure of the ear and sound transmission.
Interpret equal loudness curves and why a logarithmic scale is needed.
Use intensity level = 10 log(I/I0), I0 = 1.0e-12 W/m^2, and dB and dBA.
Explain hearing loss from noise or age using equal loudness curves.
Describe biological measurement.
Explain how an ECG is obtained and the shape of a normal ECG waveform.
Describe non-ionising imaging.
Explain reflection at tissue boundaries, acoustic impedance Z = rho c, attenuation and Ir/Ii = ((Z2-Z1)/(Z2+Z1))^2.
Describe piezoelectric generation and detection, A-scans and B-scans, and compare with other imaging.
Explain total internal reflection in fibres and flexible endoscopes with coherent and non-coherent bundles.
Explain MR scanning: proton spin alignment and precession, gradient coils, RF pulses and signal processing into images.
Describe X-ray imaging.
Explain X-ray production, maximum photon energy, continuous and characteristic spectra, and controlling intensity, energy, sharpness, contrast and dose in a rotating-anode tube.
Compare flat panel detectors with photographic detection, intensifying screens and fluoroscopy; explain contrast media like barium.
Use I = I0 e^(-mu x), mass attenuation coefficient and half-value thickness.
Describe CT principles and compare resolution, cost and safety.
Describe radionuclide imaging and therapy.
Explain tracers (Tc-99m, I-131, In-111), their properties, the Mo-Tc generator and PET scans.
Distinguish physical, biological and effective half-lives: 1/TE = 1/TB + 1/TP.
Describe the structure and operation of a photomultiplier tube and gamma camera.
Describe external treatment with high-energy X-rays and ways to limit exposure of healthy cells.
Describe internal treatment with beta-emitting implants.
Compare imaging techniques for resolution, convenience and safety.
Apply core physics to rotational dynamics and thermodynamics in engineering.
Describe rotational dynamics.
Use I = mr^2 and I = sum mr^2 and know factors affecting moment of inertia.
Use Ek = I omega^2 / 2 and explain flywheels for energy storage and smoothing torque and speed.
Use angular displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration, their graphs, and equations for uniform angular acceleration; see the analogy with linear motion.
Use T = Fr and T = I alpha.
Use angular momentum I omega, its conservation and angular impulse T change in t = change in I omega, e.g. in sport.
Use W = T theta and P = T omega and allow for frictional torque.
Describe thermodynamics and engines.
Apply Q = change in U + W quantitatively.
Treat isothermal, adiabatic, constant pressure and constant volume changes using pV = nRT, pV^gamma = constant and W = p change in V.
Represent processes on p-V diagrams and find work as area, including work per cycle as loop area.
Describe four-stroke petrol and diesel cycles and indicator diagrams.
Calculate input, indicated, brake and friction power, and overall, thermal and mechanical efficiency.
Explain the second law: heat engines need a source and sink.
Use efficiency (QH - QC)/QH and maximum efficiency (TH - TC)/TH, reasons for lower practical efficiency and CHP.
Describe heat pumps and refrigerators and calculate coefficients of performance.
Study key developments and paradigm shifts in physics.
Describe the discovery of the electron.
Describe cathode ray production in a discharge tube.
Explain thermionic emission and use mv^2/2 = eV for an accelerated electron.
Determine e/m by one method, explain Thomson's significance and compare with the hydrogen ion.
Use QV/d = mg for a stationary droplet and terminal speed with Stokes' law F = 6 pi eta r v to find droplet mass, radius and charge.
Explain quantisation of charge.
Describe the development of the wave-particle model.
Compare Newton's corpuscular theory with Huygens' wave theory and why Newton's was preferred.
Explain fringes in general terms and the delayed acceptance of the wave theory.
Use Maxwell's c = 1/sqrt(mu0 epsilon0); describe Hertz's radio waves and Fizeau's speed of light.
Describe the ultraviolet catastrophe, Planck's quanta, failure of classical theory and Einstein's explanation.
Use de Broglie's p = h/lambda and lambda = h/sqrt(2meV); explain electron diffraction changes with speed.
Estimate anode voltage for atomic-scale wavelengths and describe TEM and STM operation.
Describe special relativity.
Describe the interferometer, why it failed to detect absolute motion and the invariance of the speed of light.
State the inertial frame concept and Einstein's two postulates.
Use proper time and t = t0 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) with muon decay evidence.
Use l = l0 sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2).
Use E = mc^2 and E = m0c^2 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2); interpret mass and kinetic energy graphs and Bertozzi's experiment.
Study modern electronics from devices to data communication.
Describe discrete semiconductor devices.
Describe the N-channel enhancement MOSFET: drain, source, gate, VDS, VGS, IDSS, Vth; use as a switch and a high-input-resistance device.
Interpret zener characteristics; use with a resistor as a constant voltage source or reference.
Interpret characteristic and spectral response curves; use in photo-conductive mode and with a scintillator.
Use Hall sensors to sense magnetic field for attitude and in a tachometer.
Compare analogue and digital signals.
Use bits and bytes; explain analogue-to-digital conversion, sampling, quantisation and the effect of rate and bits on quality.
Weigh digital sampling, recovery of data from noise, pulse code modulation and sensors.
Describe analogue signal processing.
Use f0 = 1/(2 pi sqrt(LC)) for parallel resonance, the mass-spring analogy and Q = f0/fB.
Describe ideal op-amp connections, infinite open-loop gain and input resistance; use Vout = AOL(V+ - V-) and as a comparator.
Use operational amplifier configurations.
Derive and use Vout = -(Rf/Rin) Vin with virtual earth analysis.
Use Vout/Vin = 1 + Rf/Rl.
Use summing amplifier Vout = -Rf(V1/R1 + V2/R2 + ...) and difference amplifier outputs.
Describe limitations, frequency response and gain x bandwidth = constant.
Describe digital signal processing.
Use Boolean algebra, truth tables and AND, NAND, OR, NOR, NOT, EOR gates; build logic circuits from truth tables.
Describe binary, BCD and Johnson counters with clock, reset and up/down inputs, and modulo-n counters.
Describe an astable as a clock oscillator: frequency, pulse width, period, duty cycle, mark-to-space ratio and RC tuning.
Describe data communication.
Describe the stages of a real-time communication system block diagram.
Compare wire, optic fibre and radio/microwave media, wave propagation, satellite links and up/down-link frequencies, by rate, cost and security.
Describe time-division multiplexing.
Describe carrier and information signals, AM and FM waveforms and bandwidths (2fM for AM, 2 change in f + fM for FM) and channel data capacity.
